RagShortTexts: The economic sustenance of Greuthungians in 374 AD relied upon extensive agrarian estates, pastoral herds, and strategic mineral extraction.
Anchored around commercial hubs near Lower Dnieper Steppes, merchant caravans traded valuable bullion, grain, wine, and exotic raw goods.
Advanced weapon smithies and metallurgical workshops provided the industrial backbone necessary to equip large armies in the field.

Variants.Content: Underpinning the immense martial demands of Greuthungians was an agrarian and mercantile economic system rooted in rural estates and municipal workshops. Across fertile valleys and pastures, countless tenant farmers and laborers produced wheat harvests, vintage wines, cured pelts, and high-grade iron ingots destined for storehouses. Within thriving market plazas around Lower Dnieper Steppes, cosmopolitan merchants converged to barter gold coinage, imported silks, fine armaments, and livestock. Imperial or royal customs officials maintained toll gates, extracting heavy excise duties from freight wagons. Yet the system faced constant vulnerability from harvest failures and trade route disruptions, compelling rulers to enforce grain requisitions to sustain armies in the field.

The herd is counted again at dusk, and a rider wonders why the grain carts are still stuck on the rutted track. Horses, milk, and sheep are the wealth of the steppe, and every trade with the river merchants is paid in hides. He sleeps beside his mount, hoping the next market brings iron arrowheads instead of promises.

The clan chief opens his tally sticks by the fire. Horses and wool go to the trading posts on the Lower Dnieper, and each caravan owes a share to the king's household. He quietly sells two herds to a rival clan, because the king's levy always falls first on the families with the fewest herds to lose.
